html:
Ask most institutions in Rwanda’s banking and microfinance sector whether they are cyber security compliant, and the answer is almost always yes. Ask an auditor what a cyber security compliance audit in Rwanda actually turns up, and the answer looks a little different.

Suleiman Wanekeya, Operations Manager at Sentinel Africa Consulting Group, has spent years on the audit side of this question, working across ISO 27001, ISO 22301, and Rwanda’s own BNR Regulation 50 of 2022 on cyber security. Speaking at a recent Sentinel Africa Consulting webinar on the subject, he named four patterns that keep showing up, almost regardless of which institution he walks into.

1. Policy documents that say the right words, briefly

The regulation lays out roughly 16 distinct areas a cyber security policy is supposed to cover, from access control to vendor management to incident handling. What Suleiman finds in practice is policy coverage that is, in his words, very shallow, a full document that gives a single paragraph to a requirement that actually needed real depth.

It is a subtle failure. The word is there. The intent is not. And it is exactly the kind of gap that a quick read of a policy document will not catch, but a proper cyber security compliance audit in Rwanda will.

2. Penetration tests that are years overdue

The regulation expects penetration testing on a regular cycle, and Suleiman’s experience is that this is one of the most commonly missed requirements. Institutions he has audited have gone years without a test, and when a test had been done, the findings from it were often never closed out.

A test nobody acts on is close to no test at all. The value of penetration testing is not the exercise itself, it is the remediation that follows it, and that is precisely where this requirement tends to quietly die.

3. Incident reporting that exists on paper, not in practice

Regulation 50 of 2022 sets a 2 hour window for reporting a cyber incident to BNR, with a fuller report due within 24 hours. Most institutions can point to a documented process for this. Fewer can show it has ever actually been tested or exercised.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. A process that has never been rehearsed under pressure is a process nobody actually trusts when the moment arrives, whatever the document says.

4. Annual self-assessments that get copied, not redone

Every year, regulated institutions are expected to submit a self-assessment statement to BNR. What Suleiman sees, more often than institutions might expect, is last year’s assessment copied forward with minor edits, rather than genuinely reassessed against current evidence.

It is an understandable shortcut under time pressure. It is also exactly the sort of thing an auditor, or a regulator, notices immediately.

Why these four keep repeating

None of these four gaps are technical failures. They are not about weak firewalls or outdated software. They are about follow-through, about whether the organisation actually does, continuously, what its own policy says it does. That is a governance and resourcing question as much as a technical one, which is part of why Regulation 50 of 2022 places accountability for cyber security governance squarely with the board and senior management, not with IT alone.

What good evidence actually looks like

The fix is not complicated, though it does take discipline. For each of the sixteen areas the regulation covers, an institution should be able to produce actual evidence, a completed test with closed findings, a logged incident response drill, a self-assessment built from this year’s reality rather than last year’s file. If that evidence cannot be produced quickly when asked, that is usually the clearest sign of where the real gap sits, whatever the policy document says.
